questions.stem: A report page feels slow and you need to know which visual is responsible and where its time goes. What do you use first?
options: Performance analyzer in Power BI Desktop
The capacity metrics app
The refresh history of the semantic model
The lineage view of the workspace
questions.answer: Performance analyzer in Power BI Desktop
questions.explanation: Performance analyzer records each visual on the page and breaks its time into the DAX query, the visual display and other, which is exactly the information needed to know whether the problem is the model or the rendering. Capacity metrics describe the whole tenant and cannot point at one visual.
questions.sourceSkillBullet: Implement performance improvements in queries and report visuals

questions.stem: Performance analyzer reports a visual with a DAX query of 40 milliseconds and a visual display of nearly four seconds. Where is the problem?
options: In the rendering of the visual, most likely because it is being asked to draw far too many data points
In the DAX measure, which needs variables
In the data source, which is responding slowly
In the refresh schedule, which is running at the same time
questions.answer: In the rendering of the visual, most likely because it is being asked to draw far too many data points
questions.explanation: The split is the whole point of the tool. A fast query and a slow display means the model answered promptly and the visual then struggled to draw the result, which usually means too many categories or points. Optimising the DAX in this case would be effort spent on the forty milliseconds.
questions.sourceSkillBullet: Implement performance improvements in queries and report visuals

questions.stem: A page holds thirty visuals and takes a long time to open even though every individual measure is fast. What is the most likely explanation?
options: Each visual issues its own query, so thirty visuals mean thirty queries competing on open
The model must be refreshed before the page can render
Thirty visuals exceed the maximum a page may contain
The page is being rendered on the capacity rather than in the browser
questions.answer: Each visual issues its own query, so thirty visuals mean thirty queries competing on open
questions.explanation: Visual count is a cost in its own right, independent of how good any single measure is, because opening the page fires a query per visual. Reducing the number of visuals, or moving detail behind drillthrough, often does more than any amount of DAX tuning.
questions.sourceSkillBullet: Implement performance improvements in queries and report visuals

questions.stem: Which rewrite is usually faster: CALCULATE with FILTER over the whole fact table, or CALCULATE with a predicate on a single column?
options: The predicate on a single column, because FILTER over the fact table materialises far more rows
The FILTER version, because it is more explicit about intent
They are identical, because DAX rewrites one into the other
The FILTER version, because it can use the storage engine directly
questions.answer: The predicate on a single column, because FILTER over the fact table materialises far more rows
questions.explanation: A column predicate inside CALCULATE can be resolved against the values of that one column, while wrapping FILTER around the entire fact table asks the engine to iterate the fact table itself. On a large fact the difference is not subtle, and this is one of the most common causes of a slow measure.

questions.stem: A measure computes a complex total, then uses it again for a share and a third time for a variance. What is the first change to make?
options: Assign the total to a variable and reuse the variable
Split it into three separate measures
Convert it into a calculated column
Wrap each use in CALCULATE
questions.answer: Assign the total to a variable and reuse the variable
questions.explanation: Written out three times, the expensive expression may be evaluated three times. A variable computes it once and hands the same result to every use, which is the cheapest possible optimisation and also makes the measure readable. Calculated columns are computed at refresh and cannot respond to the user's filters at all.

questions.stem: A margin measure divides profit by revenue and must return blank rather than an error when revenue is zero. What is the recommended way to write it?
options: Use DIVIDE, which handles the zero case internally
Wrap the division in IFERROR
Test revenue with an IF before dividing
Filter out the zero revenue rows in the model
questions.answer: Use DIVIDE, which handles the zero case internally
questions.explanation: DIVIDE exists for exactly this and is optimised for it, returning the alternate result without the engine having to evaluate a separate guard expression for every row. An explicit IF works but adds a branch the engine must evaluate, and removing rows from the model changes the data to avoid a formatting problem.

questions.stem: What does a refresh actually do to a Direct Lake semantic model, as opposed to an import one?
options: It copies only metadata, updating the model's references to the latest files in OneLake
It reloads a full cached copy of the data, exactly as import does
It rewrites the underlying Delta tables into a new format
It clears the model so the next query has to read from the source
questions.answer: It copies only metadata, updating the model's references to the latest files in OneLake
questions.explanation: A Direct Lake refresh is framing: it analyses the metadata of the current version of the Delta tables and points the model at the latest files, which takes seconds. Import mode replicates the data into a cached copy, which is the expensive operation Direct Lake is designed to avoid.
questions.sourceSkillBullet: Configure Direct Lake, including default fallback and refresh behavior

questions.stem: You would rather a query failed visibly than quietly served an answer through DirectQuery at a different speed. Which model property controls that?
options: Direct Lake behavior
Large semantic model storage format
The refresh schedule of the model
The storage mode of each individual table
questions.explanation: The Direct Lake behavior property on the semantic model governs whether the model may fall back to DirectQuery when a query cannot be served from the Delta files directly. Setting it to refuse fallback turns an invisible performance cliff into an explicit error, which is often what a team debugging inconsistent response times actually wants.
questions.sourceSkillBullet: Configure Direct Lake, including default fallback and refresh behavior

questions.stem: Which situation causes a Direct Lake table on a SQL analytics endpoint to fall back to DirectQuery rather than reading the Delta files?
options: The data source is a SQL view, or the warehouse applies SQL based granular access control
The Delta table has been refreshed within the last hour
The report contains more than ten visuals
The model has row-level security roles defined
questions.answer: The data source is a SQL view, or the warehouse applies SQL based granular access control
questions.explanation: Fallback happens when the data simply cannot be loaded from a Delta table directly, and a view or SQL level granular access control are the documented cases: in both, the answer only exists once SQL has done some work. Knowing the triggers matters because fallback is silent by default and shows up only as a change in query time.
questions.sourceSkillBullet: Configure Direct Lake, including default fallback and refresh behavior

questions.stem: Which statement about fallback distinguishes Direct Lake on OneLake from Direct Lake on a SQL analytics endpoint?
options: Direct Lake on OneLake does not fall back to DirectQuery through the SQL analytics endpoint
Direct Lake on OneLake falls back more readily, because it reads files rather than tables
Neither of them can ever fall back to DirectQuery
Both fall back identically, and the difference is only about licensing
questions.answer: Direct Lake on OneLake does not fall back to DirectQuery through the SQL analytics endpoint
questions.explanation: Direct Lake on OneLake reads the Delta tables directly and has no SQL analytics endpoint to retreat to, so the silent fallback path does not exist for it. Direct Lake on SQL endpoints does have that path and will use it when it cannot read the Delta data directly. This is the practical difference between the two when you are reasoning about predictable query times.
questions.sourceSkillBullet: Choose between Direct Lake on OneLake and Direct Lake on SQL analytics endpoint

questions.stem: A model needs Delta tables that live in two different Fabric items, plus one small imported table from an external system. Which choice supports that?
options: Direct Lake on OneLake, which can use more than one Fabric source and allows import tables alongside
Direct Lake on a SQL analytics endpoint, which is the only mode that permits import tables
Import mode, because Direct Lake never allows more than one source
DirectQuery, because Delta tables cannot be combined at all
questions.answer: Direct Lake on OneLake, which can use more than one Fabric source and allows import tables alongside
questions.explanation: Direct Lake on OneLake can draw Delta tables from one or more Fabric data sources, and a model using it can also carry import tables from elsewhere, which makes it the mode that fits a genuinely mixed model. Reaching for import for the whole thing would work but throws away the reason for using Direct Lake.
questions.sourceSkillBullet: Choose between Direct Lake on OneLake and Direct Lake on SQL analytics endpoint

questions.stem: A warehouse enforces access with SQL based granular controls, and the reporting team needs those controls to keep applying. Which consideration follows?
options: Reading through the SQL analytics endpoint keeps those controls in play, at the cost of falling back to DirectQuery
Direct Lake on OneLake will reproduce the SQL controls automatically
Granular SQL controls are ignored by every Direct Lake mode
The controls must be removed before any Direct Lake model can be built
questions.answer: Reading through the SQL analytics endpoint keeps those controls in play, at the cost of falling back to DirectQuery
questions.explanation: SQL based granular access control is one of the documented reasons a Direct Lake table on a SQL analytics endpoint falls back to DirectQuery: the restriction is enforced by SQL, so SQL has to be involved. That is a real trade, security semantics against the direct read, and it is the kind of decision this skill is asking you to make deliberately rather than discover later.
questions.sourceSkillBullet: Choose between Direct Lake on OneLake and Direct Lake on SQL analytics endpoint

questions.stem: Which two parameters must exist before an incremental refresh policy can be configured on a table?
options: RangeStart and RangeEnd, both of date and time type
StartDate and EndDate, both of text type
PeriodFrom and PeriodTo, both whole numbers
RefreshFrom and RefreshTo, both of date type
questions.answer: RangeStart and RangeEnd, both of date and time type
questions.explanation: The names and the data type are both fixed requirements: the policy looks for parameters called RangeStart and RangeEnd of date and time type, and the table's query must filter on them. Getting either the name or the type wrong is the usual reason the incremental refresh option stays greyed out.
questions.sourceSkillBullet: Implement incremental refresh for semantic models

questions.stem: A policy archives five years of data and refreshes the last ten days. What happens on a scheduled refresh?
options: Only the partitions covering the last ten days are reprocessed, and the archived years are left alone
All five years are reloaded, but more quickly than before
The archived years are deleted and reloaded from the source
Nothing is reloaded until the ten day window has fully elapsed
questions.answer: Only the partitions covering the last ten days are reprocessed, and the archived years are left alone
questions.explanation: That is the entire benefit. Splitting the table into partitions by date lets the refresh touch only the recent ones, so the run gets shorter and the load on the source falls, while the history stays in the model without being fetched again.
questions.sourceSkillBullet: Implement incremental refresh for semantic models

questions.stem: Incremental refresh has been configured correctly, yet every run still pulls the entire history from the source. What should you suspect first?
options: The query does not fold, so the date filter is never pushed down to the source
The archive period is set too short
The model needs the large storage format enabled
The refresh is scheduled too frequently
questions.answer: The query does not fold, so the date filter is never pushed down to the source
questions.explanation: Incremental refresh partitions the model correctly either way, but the saving only reaches the source if the RangeStart and RangeEnd filter folds into the query sent to it. When folding breaks, typically because of an earlier transformation, the whole table is fetched and then filtered locally, which is the expensive half of what the feature was meant to avoid.
questions.sourceSkillBullet: Implement incremental refresh for semantic models
